plain_title: When a flaw nobody else sees takes over your life
one_liner: Being consumed by a perceived flaw in your appearance that others don't see or barely notice.
in_simple_words: Body dysmorphic disorder is far more than disliking how you look. A person becomes convinced that some part of their appearance, often skin, nose, hair, or body shape, is ugly or deformed, when others see nothing or only something minor. They spend hours checking mirrors, comparing, grooming, or hiding, and may avoid people, work, or school. The distress is severe and the condition carries a high suicide risk. It is treatable, with therapy and medication, and it isn't vanity.
what_it_can_feel_like: I'd check the mirror two hundred times a day and every time it was worse.
Everyone said I looked fine. I thought they were being kind. It took years to see that I was the one not seeing clearly.
Treatment didn't make me love my face. It gave me my days back.
common_signs: Constant worry about a flaw others don't see or think is small
Hours spent checking mirrors, grooming, comparing, or seeking reassurance
Hiding the 'flaw' with clothes, makeup, posture, or avoiding people
Seeking cosmetic procedures that rarely help
Distress severe enough to disrupt work, school, or relationships
In muscle dysmorphia, believing you're too small despite being muscular

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's just vanity or low self-esteem.
myths_vs_facts.fact: BDD is a serious condition with severe distress and one of the highest suicide rates in mental health. It has nothing to do with vanity.
Procedures rarely help BDD and often make it worse, shifting the focus to a new 'flaw'. Surgeons are advised to screen for BDD first.
It affects men and women almost equally. In men it often takes the form of muscle dysmorphia.

how_common.plain: About 2 in 100 people have BDD, making it more common than many people realize. It usually starts in the teens.
how_common.figure: Point prevalence about 1.7%–2.4% in general-population studies (Germany and the US)

what_helps.plain_summary: CBT designed specifically for BDD, which includes exposure and response prevention for mirror checking, hiding, and reassurance seeking, is the first-line treatment. Antidepressants (SSRIs), prescribed and monitored by a doctor, often at higher doses, help many people and are combined with CBT for more severe BDD. Cosmetic procedures are not a treatment. For young people, family-involved CBT comes first.
evidence_based_options: CBT developed for BDD, including exposure and response prevention
SSRI antidepressants, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Combined CBT and medication for severe BDD
Family-involved CBT for children and teenagers
self_help_that_supports_care: Cutting down mirror checking gradually, with a plan
Dropping one hiding or camouflaging behaviour at a time
Peer support with others who have BDD, which breaks the isolation

when_to_reach_out: If worry about your appearance takes up hours a day, stops you going out, or makes you think about cosmetic procedures or ending your life, talk to a doctor or therapist and mention BDD by name. If you're having thoughts of suicide, use the crisis strip now.
is_not: Disliking a feature, wanting to look good, or ordinary teenage self-consciousness isn't BDD. Fear of being fat with restricted eating is more likely an eating disorder, though the two can overlap.
hope_note: People with BDD recover. The mirror stops being a battlefield, and the hours come back.
in_young_people: BDD usually starts around 12 to 13 and is often hidden behind 'teenage insecurity'. Refusing school, long bathroom routines, and intense distress about photos can be signs. Early treatment prevents years of lost life.
across_cultures: The feature people focus on varies: skin tone, hair texture, eye shape, nose, body build. Beauty norms, colourism, and social media shape what feels 'wrong'. BDD is found worldwide.

sub_sections.title: Muscle dysmorphia
sub_sections.text: A form of BDD, mostly in men, where a person believes they're too small or not muscular enough despite being lean or muscular. It can drive extreme exercise, rigid diets, and steroid use.

sub_sections.title: BDD by proxy
sub_sections.text: Rarely, the obsession is with a perceived flaw in someone else's appearance, such as a partner or child.

content_notes: High suicide risk in BDD; crisis strip required.
No body descriptions, measurements, or 'before/after' framing.
Illustration must not show mirrors with distorted reflections or bodies being scrutinized.
